headline: Dry and warm through Friday, with Thanksgiving highs 10–15 degrees above average and gusty northeast winds near the mountains, while record King Tides and a big incoming swell bring major, locally extreme coastal flooding to the Orange and San Diego County coasts through Friday; a cooler, possibly much wetter pattern follows early next week.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Tuesday is warmer, with highs on the coast and in the valleys up 4–8 degrees, mostly into the 70s, and the deserts a few degrees warmer still. Weak offshore flow (dry winds blowing from inland toward the coast) brings east winds gusting to about 35 mph along and below the coast-facing mountain slopes in Riverside and San Diego counties, easing by late morning. High clouds passing over early Tuesday clear out by late morning, and it stays dry.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: On Wednesday a weak low-pressure system moving inland through Baja and Southern California weakens the offshore winds, with little change in coast and valley temperatures and the deserts a few degrees warmer. High pressure strengthens for Thanksgiving (Thursday), bringing stronger offshore winds, with northeast to east gusts of 35–45 mph along and below the coastal mountain slopes and through the passes. Thanksgiving highs climb another 4–8 degrees on the coast and in the valleys, 10–15 degrees above average, reaching the lower to mid 80s from inland coastal areas into the western valleys.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Friday is about as warm or slightly warmer, with highs around 80 near the coast and in the lower to mid 80s in the valleys and inland coastal areas, and still dry. Cooling spreads inland Saturday, down 5–10 degrees to mostly the 70s, and another 5 degrees or so Sunday, to the upper 60s to mid 70s on the coast and in the valleys. A fast-moving low-pressure system could bring some rain Sunday into Sunday night, and a more substantial storm is possible next Tuesday and Wednesday: the chance of 1 inch or more of rain is 55–65 percent from the coast to the mountains, the chance of 2 inches or more is about 25–35 percent near the coast and 45–55 percent in the San Bernardino County mountains, and there is a 5–10 percent chance of 5 inches or more in those mountains.

coast: Coastal flooding is the big hazard this week on the Orange County and San Diego County coasts. Morning high tides already reached 7.73 feet at La Jolla (its third-highest on record) and 8.24 feet at the San Diego Broadway Pier on Monday, and will climb to 7.9–8.3 feet Tuesday through Thursday, peaking Wednesday, about 1.1–1.2 feet above normal predictions and likely breaking the all-time records set in late October. Surf stays around 2–5 feet through Wednesday morning, then a large, long-period west swell (8–9 feet every 18–19 seconds) arrives late Wednesday into Thursday, bringing 6–8 foot breakers Thursday with sets of 10–12 feet on exposed west-facing beaches, lowering to 3–6 feet Friday. A Coastal Flood Warning runs from 4 AM Tuesday to 1 PM Friday for major flooding, with locally extreme flooding expected at Thursday morning's high tide, and a High Surf Advisory covers the San Diego County coast from 1 PM Wednesday to 4 AM Friday. Ocean water is unusually warm: 73.2°F at Scripps Pier Monday, 11.6 degrees above average. For boaters, no hazards are expected Tuesday; a Small Craft Advisory covers the outer waters (10–60 miles out, including San Clemente Island) from 10 AM Wednesday to 10 AM Thursday for combined seas of 8–12 feet and northwest winds of about 23–29 mph (20–25 knots) near San Clemente Island Wednesday afternoon and evening, with seas falling below 10 feet by Thursday evening.
watch_for: Major, locally extreme coastal flooding at the morning high tides through Friday, worst Thursday when record tides meet 10–12 foot surf sets.
Gusty, dry northeast winds of 35–45 mph near the mountains and passes on Thanksgiving and Friday, with highs in the 80s inland.
A possibly substantial storm next Tuesday and Wednesday, with a better-than-even chance of an inch or more of rain from the coast to the mountains.
confidence: Forecasters are confident in the dry, warm weather through Friday and in the record tides and coastal flooding; the chance of rain Sunday is uncertain, and the heavier storm next Tuesday and Wednesday is described only as possible, with probabilities rather than firm amounts.
